chapter: Syndromes of the head and neck

coreTruths.title: Head and neck signs can be the first window on serious systemic disease
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most named syndromes are rare, but a handful are clinically worthwhile because a routine oral or facial finding flags hidden disease elsewhere that needs urgent action.
coreTruths.body:
## The point of learning the names is pattern recognition, not trivia

The value of knowing head and neck syndromes is not the eponym itself. It is being able to spot the pattern at the chair, name it, and act on it before the underlying disease declares itself somewhere else [1]. A few entries in this group are flagged as genuinely worthwhile, and they share a feature: a small oral or facial sign that mandates investigation of a distant organ.

## Some oral findings mandate looking outside the mouth

Facial osteomas on a panoramic film are not just bony lumps. In Gardener syndrome they sit alongside polyps of the large intestine that have a tendency to rapid malignant change, so the radiographic finding mandates examination of the lower GI tract [2]. Mucosal neuromas in a tall, thin, wasted-looking young patient can be MEN IIb, which carries medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma; biopsy is mandatory and a suggestive histology means the thyroid must be investigated [3]. A new Horner pattern (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis) can be the first sign of a bronchogenic carcinoma invading the cervical sympathetic chain [4].

## Some oral findings flag a premalignant lesion that the patient can be saved from

A middle-aged woman with dysphagia, microcytic anaemia, koilonychia, and angular cheilitis fits Patterson-Brown-Kelly. The post-cricoid web behind the dysphagia is premalignant, and correcting the anaemia can both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression [5]. Late-onset parotid swelling in a Sjogren patient can herald a lymphoma [6]. The recurring lesson is that the dental chair sees these patients before anyone else does.

## Refer wide, not just up

Many of these conditions are multisystem from the start. Behcet's is described as a multisystem disease of immunological origin where the job is to recognise and refer for multidisciplinary care [7]. Treating the oral ulcers without flagging the eyes, skin, and joints misses the point of the diagnosis.

citations.quote: The real importance behind the learning of names associated with conditions which may be of relevance to, or be picked up by, clinical examination of the head and neck, is that, once learned, some difficult diagnostic problems can be quickly solved and appropriate Rx instituted.

This comprises multiple osteomas (particularly of the jaws and facial bones), multiple polyps of the large intestine, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas of the skin. It shows autosomal dominant inheritance. The discovery on clinical or X-ray examination of facial osteomas mandates examination of the lower gastrointestinal tract, as these polyps have a tendency to rapid malignant change. This is a highly 'worthwhile' syndrome.

MEN IIb is of particular relevance as it consists of multiple mucosal neuromas which have a characteristic histopathology, phaeochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and a thin wasted appearance. Calcitonin levels are elevated if medullary thyroid carcinoma is present. Index of suspicion should be high in tall, thin, wasted-looking children and young adults presenting with lumps in the mouth. Biopsy is mandatory and if histopathology is suggestive the thyroid must be adequately investigated. This is another 'worthwhile' syndrome.

Consists of a constricted pupil (miosis), drooping eyelid (ptosis), unilateral loss of sweating (anhidrosis) on the face, and occasionally sunken eye (enophthalmos). It is caused by interruption of sympathetic nerve fibres at the cervical ganglion 2° to, e.g. bronchogenic carcinoma, invading the ganglion or neck trauma. Scores high on the 'worthwhile' rating.

The dysphagia is due to a post-cricoid web, usually a membrane on the anterior oesophageal wall, which is premalignant. The koilonychia and angular cheilitis are 2° to the anaemia but may be presenting symptoms. The main affected group is middle-aged women, and correction of the anaemia may both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression of the web.

In addition to dry eyes and dry mouth this has both the serology and symptomatology of an autoimmune condition, usually rheumatoid arthritis, but sometimes SLE, systemic sclerosis, or 1° biliary cholangitis. Actual swelling of the salivary glands is relatively uncommon and late-onset swelling of the parotids may herald the presence of a lymphoma.
It is, in fact, a multisystem disease of immunological origin—need to recognize and refer for multidisciplinary care.
